text.p: The following are some of the leading stories in Finnish papers this morning.
HELSINGIN SANOMAT

- Strikes at Canadian paper factories may be long-needed shot-in-the-arm for global pulp and paper markets: if they last, they can balance demand and supply globally and hike paper and pulp prices, Finnish sector representatives say.
- Trade between Finland and Russia has doubled from early 1990s; small- and middle sized companies selling food and consumption goods have replaced major flows. @
- Secondary markets for bank loans rooting from Soviet period has livened up, Finnish banks have sold loans forward to international banks with 70-85 percent par value.
- Central Union of Agricultural Producers and Forest Owners (MTK) plans to start charging urban forest owners for lobbying.
- Privacy protection authorities have asked police to investigate whether old Communist Party's privacy was violated when secret achives collected by the state police in late 1940s were published.
- This year Finns have been losing their lives in water at record speed, over 100 have already drowned. @

- After a boom in the 1970s and 1980s, Finns have disappeared from top U.N positions. Now jobs in the European Union are found more interesting, says Finland's permanent U.N representative Wilhelm Breitenstein.
KAUPPALEHTI
- After summer holidays, the markka may face speculative pressures, forcing Bank of Finland to intervene to prevent it strengthening, economists say.
- State-owned railway company VR's monopoly on rails is against EU directives and overall Finnish traffic policy is far from being equal, representatives of bus business say. @
- A quick transition from markka to euro would cause major problems for automatic teller and other self-service machine companies, sector representatives say.
AAMULEHTI
- Stampede after visa requirements between Estonia and Finland ended in May has been Finns to Estonia, not vice versa as expected. @
TURUN SANOMAT

- International telecommunication countries say satellite telephone to challenge mobile phones in future: Nokia follows developments in satellite phones, but does not have any concrete plans, company spokesperson says.
HUFVUDSTADSBLADET
- Traffic information by satellite could clear up traffic jams at eastern border of Finland, logistics developers say.
--Nora Hallberg, Helsinki Newsroom +358-9-680 50 292
